author: high3
claim: Upper-bound subgoal solved: every red-blue coloring of the edges of the complete graph on six vertices contains a monochromatic triangle.
evidence: Choose a vertex v. Its five incident edges use two colors, so at least three have one common color. Let their other endpoints be a,b,c. If one of ab,bc,ca has that common color, it and v form a monochromatic triangle. If none does, then ab,bc,ca all have the other color, so abc is monochromatic.

links.attempt_summary: Pigeonhole at one vertex, followed by the two exhaustive color cases inside the chosen three neighbors.

glossary.a: one of three neighbors joined to v in a common color
glossary.b: one of three neighbors joined to v in a common color
glossary.c: one of three neighbors joined to v in a common color

author: high3
claim: Lower-bound subgoal solved: there is a red-blue coloring of the complete graph on five vertices containing no monochromatic triangle.
evidence: Label the vertices 0,1,2,3,4 modulo 5. Color an edge red when its endpoint labels differ by 1 modulo 5 up to sign, and blue when they differ by 2 modulo 5 up to sign. At any vertex i, its two red neighbors i-1 and i+1 differ by 2 and hence their joining edge is blue. Its two blue neighbors i-2 and i+2 differ by 1 modulo 5 up to sign and hence their joining edge is red. Thus a monochromatic triangle of either color is impossible.

links.attempt_summary: Explicit cyclic coloring, with the edge between the two same-colored neighbors of every vertex forced to have the opposite color.

author: high6
claim: Direct upper-bound subgoal solved: every red-blue coloring of the complete graph on six vertices contains a monochromatic triangle.
evidence: Plan upper-lower, direct attempt. Choose any vertex v. Of its five incident edges, at least three have one common color by the pigeonhole principle; call their other endpoints x,y,z and call the common color C. If one of xy,xz,yz has color C, it and v form a C-colored triangle. If none has color C, then all three have the other color, so xyz is a monochromatic triangle. Status=solved; counterexample search not needed; no external result used.

glossary.v: an arbitrary vertex of the six-vertex complete graph
glossary.x,y,z: three distinct neighbors of v joined to v in one common color
glossary.C: the common color of the edges from v to x, y, and z

author: high6
claim: Direct lower-bound subgoal solved: the complete graph on five vertices has a red-blue edge coloring with no monochromatic triangle.
evidence: Plan upper-lower, direct attempt. Label the vertices 0,1,2,3,4. Color red precisely the edges of the cycle 0-1-2-3-4-0. The remaining edges are 0-2,2-4,4-1,1-3,3-0, so they form the blue cycle 0-2-4-1-3-0. A cycle of length five has no triangle: at each vertex its two neighbors on that cycle are not adjacent in the cycle. Hence neither color class contains a triangle. Status=solved; counterexample search not needed; no external result used.

author: high2
claim: Upper-bound subgoal solved: every red-blue edge-coloring of the complete graph on six vertices contains a monochromatic triangle.
evidence: Choose any vertex v. Its five incident edges have two colors, so at least three have one common color. Name their other endpoints a,b,c. If the common color is red and one of ab,ac,bc is red, that edge with v forms a red triangle; if none is red, all three are blue and abc is a blue triangle. If the common color is blue, exchange the words red and blue in the same exhaustive argument. Thus every coloring contains a monochromatic triangle.

links.attempt_summary: Pigeonhole at one vertex, followed by an exhaustive dichotomy on the triangle among three same-colored neighbors.

counterexample_search_for_stuck_subgoal.summary: Not needed because the direct proof closed.

glossary.a: One endpoint joined to v in the selected common color.
glossary.b: A second endpoint joined to v in the selected common color.
glossary.c: A third endpoint joined to v in the selected common color.

author: high2
claim: Lower-bound subgoal solved: there is a red-blue edge-coloring of the complete graph on five vertices with no monochromatic triangle.
evidence: Label the vertices 0,1,2,3,4 modulo 5. Color an edge red exactly when its endpoint difference is congruent to 1 or -1 modulo 5; color all remaining edges blue, equivalently those with difference 2 or -2. For any vertex i, its two red neighbors are i-1 and i+1; their difference is 2 modulo 5, so their mutual edge is blue. Therefore no triangle through i can have all three edges red, and hence there is no red triangle. Its two blue neighbors are i-2 and i+2; their difference is 4, congruent to -1 modulo 5, so their mutual edge is red. Therefore no triangle through i can have all three edges blue, and hence there is no blue triangle.

links.attempt_summary: Color a 5-cycle red and its complementary 5-cycle blue; inspect the two same-colored neighbors of an arbitrary vertex.
used_examples: The red 5-cycle and its complementary blue 5-cycle.

counterexample_search_for_stuck_subgoal.summary: Not needed because the explicit construction was proved valid.

author: high
claim: Subgoal solved: every red-blue coloring of the edges of the complete graph on six vertices contains a monochromatic triangle.
evidence: Choose any vertex v. Exactly five edges are incident with v. If neither color occurred on at least three of these edges, each color would occur at most twice, accounting for at most four incident edges, a contradiction. Hence for one color gamma there are three distinct other vertices x, y, z such that vx, vy, vz all have color gamma. If at least one of xy, yz, zx has color gamma, that edge together with v gives a triangle all of whose edges have color gamma. If none has color gamma, then xy, yz, zx all have the other color, so x, y, z form a monochromatic triangle.

links.attempt_summary: Degree-five pigeonhole split, followed by the two exhaustive possibilities for the triangle on the three same-color neighbors.

glossary.gamma: one of the two edge colors, red or blue
glossary.x: one endpoint other than v of an edge of color gamma incident with v

author: high
claim: Subgoal solved: there is a red-blue coloring of the edges of the complete graph on five vertices containing no monochromatic triangle.
evidence: Label the vertices by residues 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 modulo 5. Color two distinct vertices red exactly when their difference is congruent to 1 or -1 modulo 5, and blue exactly when their difference is congruent to 2 or -2 modulo 5. These alternatives partition all unordered pairs of distinct residues. Suppose a red triangle contained a vertex a. Its two other vertices would have to be the two red neighbors a+1 and a-1, but their difference is 2 modulo 5, so their edge is blue. Suppose a blue triangle contained a. Its two other vertices would have to be the two blue neighbors a+2 and a-2, but their difference is 4, congruent to -1 modulo 5, so their edge is red. Both suppositions are impossible.

links.attempt_summary: Color the 5-cycle red and its complementary 5-cycle blue; inspect the two same-color neighbors of any chosen vertex.
used_examples: The red 5-cycle and its blue complement.

glossary.a: an arbitrary vertex label, interpreted modulo 5

author: high5
claim: Complete target solved directly: every red-blue coloring of the edges of the complete graph on six vertices contains a monochromatic triangle, while an explicit red-blue coloring of the complete graph on five vertices contains no monochromatic triangle; hence R(3,3)=6.
evidence: Upper bound: choose a vertex v of a six-vertex complete graph. Of the five edges incident with v, at least three share a color by the pigeonhole principle. Let their other endpoints be a,b,c. If any of ab,bc,ca has that same color, it forms with v a triangle all of whose edges have that color. If none has that color, then, since there are exactly two colors, ab,bc,ca all have the other color, so abc is monochromatic. Lower bound: label five vertices 0,1,2,3,4. Color 01,12,23,34,40 red and color the other five edges 02,24,41,13,30 blue. The red edges form the cycle 0-1-2-3-4-0, and the blue edges form the cycle 0-2-4-1-3-0. A five-cycle has no triangle: at each vertex its only two neighbors on the cycle are not joined by an edge of that cycle. Thus neither color contains a triangle. The upper and lower bounds give R(3,3)=6 by its definition as the least vertex count forcing a monochromatic triangle.

counterexample_search_for_stuck_subgoal.summary: No subgoal was stuck; both were proved directly.

glossary.v: an arbitrarily chosen vertex of the complete graph on six vertices
glossary.a: one of three neighbors joined to v by edges of one common color
glossary.b: one of three neighbors joined to v by edges of one common color
glossary.c: one of three neighbors joined to v by edges of one common color
glossary.R(3,3): the least positive integer n such that every red-blue coloring of the edges of the complete graph on n vertices contains a monochromatic triangle
